displayQuote: We Are Never Alone. Not When the Night Is Darkest, the Wind Coldest

meta.title: Who really said "We Are Never Alone. Not When the Night Is Darkest, the Wind Coldest"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Taylor Caldwell wrote it. The line closes her autobiographical story "My Christmas Miracle," published in Family Circle on 24 December 1961.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We Are Never Alone. Not When the Night Is Darkest, the Wind Coldest'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Taylor Caldwell — the closing sentence of her 1961 Family Circle story "My Christmas Miracle," not a novel and not an anonymous card verse.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing lines of Caldwell’s autobiographical story “My Christmas Miracle,” which Quote Investigator ↗ traces to Family Circle, 24 December 1961. The full story — ending on this exact sentence — is reproduced in the publisher’s own sample text for the 1996 Guideposts anthology Christmas in My Heart, hosted by the Library of Congress ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Christmas in My Heart, comp. and ed. Joe Wheeler (Carmel, NY: Guideposts, 1996), 209–14

source.excerpt:
“The Lord is born!” sang the bells to the crystal night and the laughing darkness. Someone began to sing, “Come, all ye faithful!” I joined in and sang with the strangers all about me.

I am not alone at all, I thought. I was never alone at all.

And that, of course, is the message of Christmas. We are never alone. Not when the night is darkest, the wind coldest, the world seemingly most indifferent. For this is still the time God chooses.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ investigated the line in December 2012 and identified it as the ending of Caldwell’s autobiographical story “My Christmas Miracle,” published in Family Circle on 24 December 1961 and reprinted in Christmas in My Heart (Guideposts, 1996) at pages 209–14, with the quotation on page 214.
The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for that 1996 Guideposts volume ↗ lists its contents, including “My Christmas miracle / Taylor Caldwell.”

The publisher-supplied sample text for the same book, hosted by the Library of Congress ↗, reproduces the story in full — from the umbrella found on the streetcar to the final sentence, which is the quotation.

Wikiquote’s Caldwell page ↗ lists her quotations by decade and does not include this line in any section, which is consistent with the reader’s report to Quote Investigator that the words had only ever sat in an “Unsourced” list.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the publisher’s sample text for Christmas in My Heart (Guideposts, 1996) hosted by the Library of Congress. Note the reading “the world seemingly most indifferent”: Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ of the same passage prints “the word.”

author.name: Taylor Caldwell
author.heading: Who was Taylor Caldwell?
author.metaLine: 1900–1985 · Anglo-American novelist of historical & religious fiction
author.bio: Born Janet Miriam Caldwell in Manchester, England, in 1900 — Taylor Caldwell was itself a pen name — she emigrated as a child and spent most of her life in and around Buffalo, New York. She wrote sprawling historical and religious novels — Dynasty of Death, Dear and Glorious Physician, Captains and the Kings — that sold in the tens of millions, and she also published under the pen names Marcus Holland and Max Reiner. Before any of that she did clerical work in Buffalo: court reporter for the New York State Department of Labor in 1923–24, then secretary to a federal immigration tribunal. The Christmas story recalls a version of herself from those years, though its chronology and the documented record do not line up (see the note above).

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — unusually, for a line this quotable. What goes wrong is everything around it: the wording drifts, the source vanishes, and one reprint’s layout makes the sentence look like an editor’s afterthought rather than Caldwell’s own ending.

items.why: The publisher’s own sample text ↗ reads “the world seemingly most indifferent,” and so does the full story at christmasstories.org ↗. The transcription on Quote Investigator ↗ prints “the word.” Reprints do not follow it: Goodreads and AZQuotes both read “world,” as do all three full texts above. “World” is what the story says.

The Buffalo History Gazette reprint ↗ places a captioned portrait of “Taylor Caldwell (Janet Reback)” immediately before the closing paragraph in the page source — a floated table a browser draws to the right of the text — so text extractors and screen readers meet the name just ahead of the famous lines, and they read as a note added afterwards. In the publisher’s text the paragraph runs on unbroken as the last words of Caldwell’s own story.

The reader who wrote to Quote Investigator in 2012 reported finding the line only in the “Unsourced” section of Wikiquote. It is not on the Wikiquote page at all today ↗, and quote aggregators still reprint it with a bare name and no work — which is how a genuine, datable sentence ends up looking like a fabrication.

misattribution.truthLine: It is really Caldwell, and it really has a source: the last paragraph of “My Christmas Miracle,” first published in Family Circle on 24 December 1961 ↗ and reprinted in Christmas in My Heart (Guideposts, 1996).

context.heading: Why it lands
lead: It reads like a greeting-card line, which is exactly why it gets treated as one. In its actual setting it is the last sentence of a hard little memoir. Caldwell describes herself as “recently divorced, I was in my 20s,” with no job, a small daughter, three cans of food for that night’s dinner and only hamburgers and gelatin promised for Christmas, and, in her own words, a moment when “for the first time in my life, I doubted the existence of God and His mercy.”

The story turns on an umbrella. She finds an expensive one on a Buffalo streetcar, tracks down its owner — a schoolteacher — and refuses a reward she badly needs. Months later, at her lowest, a delivery man arrives with parcels from that teacher, and the same evening’s post brings a bonus cheque and a job offer. The famous sentence is the conclusion she draws, not a maxim she set out to write.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the story’s internal chronology
detailsBody: Caldwell’s telling places the events in her twenties and describes her as recently divorced, with a daughter “not yet 6 years old.” Wikipedia’s biography dates the birth of her daughter Mary Margaret (“Peggy”) to 1920 and her divorce from William Combs to 1931. Those details do not reconcile cleanly, and the memoir was written many years after the events it describes.
Quotle.info has not resolved that discrepancy and therefore puts no year on the Christmas the story recounts. What is documented is the date of publication, not the date of the events.
context.pull: It is a conclusion drawn at the end of a bad year, not an aphorism.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quotation to Taylor Caldwell's autobiographical story "My Christmas Miracle," published in Family Circle on 24 December 1961, and cites the reprint in Christmas in My Heart (Guideposts, 1996), pages 209-214 with the quotation at 214; QI's own transcription of the passage prints "the word seemingly most indifferent"; the questioner reported finding the line only in Wikiquote's "Unsourced" section.

The Library of Congress-hosted publisher sample text for "Christmas in my heart ... compiled and edited by Joe Wheeler" (LCCN 96025672) reproduces Taylor Caldwell's "My Christmas Miracle" in full, including the umbrella found on the streetcar, the teacher's parcels, the $30 Christmas bonus and the government job offer, and ends with the exact sentence "And that, of course, is the message of Christmas. We are never alone. Not when the night is darkest, the wind coldest, the world seemingly most indifferent. For this is still the time God chooses." The story also contains the line "Recently divorced, I was in my 20s."

The Internet Archive catalogue record for Christmas in my heart gives publisher "Carmel, NY : Guideposts", date 1996, compiler Joe L. Wheeler, and a contents list that includes "My Christmas miracle / Taylor Caldwell".

The Buffalo History Gazette (24 December 2010) reprints the full text of "My Christmas Miracle", reads "the world seemingly most indifferent", and places a captioned portrait labelled "Taylor Caldwell (Janet Reback)" (a tr-caption-container table styled float: right) immediately before the closing paragraph beginning "And that, of course, is the message of Christmas." in the page source.

christmasstories.org reprints "My Christmas Miracle" credited to Taylor Caldwell, without giving an original publication, and its final paragraph reads "the world seemingly most indifferent" (not "the word").

Wikiquote's Taylor Caldwell page gives her dates as September 7, 1900 - August 30, 1985, names her Janet Miriam Holland Taylor Caldwell with pen names Marcus Holland and Max Reiner, organises quotations by decade, and contains no occurrence of "never alone" or "coldest" and no "Unsourced" section.

Wikipedia gives Taylor Caldwell's birth as 7 September 1900 in Manchester, England, her death as 30 August 1985 in Greenwich, Connecticut, describes her as a British-born American novelist of historical and religious fiction (Dynasty of Death, Dear and Glorious Physician, Captains and the Kings), records her life near Buffalo, her marriage to William F. Combs in 1919, daughter Mary Margaret "Peggy" born 1920, and their divorce in 1931.
